title: License Conditions That Limit the Ability of Foreign Firms: Export Gatekeeping in Nvidia's Own Filing
participants: Government of the People's Republic of China

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim is the margin and the disclosure is the company's own: "Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year ago and up 18% sequentially", and gross margin "increased to 75.0% for the second quarter of fiscal year 2027 compared to 72.4% for the second quarter of fiscal year 2026". Seventy-five cents of gross margin on the dollar, in a quarter when the market for the same products in the largest competing economy was closed in both directions.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is a licence regime written in the physics of the product. "The export controls applicable to China are complex and address a variety of parameters, including the total processing performance of a chip, the 'performance density' of a chip, the interconnect bandwidth of a chip, and the memory bandwidth of a chip." A threshold expressed in bandwidth and processing density is a line that only the designer can be sure of standing on, which makes the compliance boundary and the product roadmap the same document.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The company discloses the fog rather than resolving it: of the replacement for the rescinded AI Diffusion rule, "The scope, timing, and requirements of the forthcoming rule remain uncertain", and the government "has changed and may again change the export control rules at any time". Meanwhile licences granted on one side were blocked on the other: "Beginning in August 2025, the USG granted licenses that would have allowed us to ship certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, but such sales were restricted by the PRC government, and we were unable to sell our H20 inventory." The same thing happened again with H200 from February 2026.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The condition worth reading twice is not about chips at all; it is about who may run a cluster. In the company's words: "the USG already imposed license conditions that limit the ability of foreign firms to create and offer as a service large-scale GPU clusters, such as imposing license conditions on the use of products to be exported to certain countries". An export licence that reaches past the sale and into the buyer's business model is the gatekeeping the node is named for. Alongside it, the concentration on the demand side is disclosed too: "For the first half of fiscal year 2027, three direct customers represented 16%, 15%, and 13% of total revenue".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There is no inquiry in this record and no proceeding; what there is, is a cost booked and a position stated. The H20 episode produced provisions "including $4.5 billion associated with H20 excess inventory", and the company's filed position is that it is the party harmed: "Export controls have and are likely in the future to have a disproportionate impact on NVIDIA and may disadvantage us against certain of our competitors that sell chips that are outside the scope of such control."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Four years of accreting export restrictions, dated in the filing: August 2022 restrictions targeting China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries; October 2023 licensing requirements extended to Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 — "including but not limited to, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Vietnam, but excluding Israel"; and April 2025 licensing for H20 and anything above the stated thresholds to China, Hong Kong, Macau and D:5 countries or companies ultimately parented there.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A new commercial structure disclosed in the same filing: "a new business model with certain select AI cloud partners" under which "AI clouds procure our data center infrastructure products and we commit to cloud service agreements", commitments "typically six years in duration" totalling "$36 billion as of July 26, 2026", with the company participating in "revenue share generated by the AI clouds from third-party customers" if criteria are met. Compute sold, then rented back, then shared in.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Licensing thresholds defined by chip performance make the vendor the arbiter of what is exportable; the vendor designs to the threshold; licences then condition what foreign buyers may do with what they bought, including offering clusters as a service; the restricted market's own government blocks the licensed sales anyway; the unsold inventory is written down; and the same quarter's margin rises to 75% because the unrestricted demand is concentrated in three customers who have nowhere else to go.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Nvidia operates a GPU cartel with the United States government's blessing, and pays for the privilege by handing Washington a cut — fifteen percent of its China revenue — making export control a revenue-sharing agreement between a monopolist and a state.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: THE REVENUE-SHARE CLAIM IS NOT IN THE COMPANY'S OWN FILING, AND THE FULL TEXT WAS SEARCHED FOR IT. There is no mention of any payment, remittance or revenue share to the United States government or to any government. The strings "remit", "payment to the U.S", "to the USG" and "equity stake" do not appear anywhere in the document. The only "15%" in the filing is a customer-concentration figure — "three direct customers represented 16%, 15%, and 13% of total revenue". And the only revenue share disclosed is with commercial counterparties: "If certain criteria are met, we will participate in revenue share generated by the AI clouds from third-party customers" — the company receiving a share from AI cloud partners, not paying one to a state. The word "cartel" does not appear either, no agreement with any competitor is disclosed, and no antitrust proceeding appears in the passages read. The node's original title asserted sovereign revenue; that has been replaced, because nothing read supports it. WHAT THE FILING DOES ESTABLISH IS THE GATEKEEPING, and it is stronger evidence than the rumour because the company says it against its own interest, under securities law. Export licences have conditioned not just the sale but the use: "the USG already imposed license conditions that limit the ability of foreign firms to create and offer as a service large-scale GPU clusters". The thresholds are written in the product's own physics — total processing performance, performance density, interconnect bandwidth, memory bandwidth. The rules "have changed and may again change ... at any time" and the replacement for the rescinded AI Diffusion rule is of "uncertain" scope. And the gate closes from both ends: licences granted in August 2025 for H20 and in February 2026 for H200 were made worthless by PRC restrictions, costing $4.5 billion in H20 inventory provisions. The company's filed position is that it is the loser — export controls "have and are likely in the future to have a disproportionate impact on NVIDIA" — which may be true and still leave intact the thing this dossier records: a market in which one firm's product specifications define a national licensing boundary, three customers account for 44% of revenue, and gross margin is 75%.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: NVIDIA Corporation's Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 26 July 2026, filed 26 August 2026. It discloses: export restrictions announced by the US government in August 2022 targeting China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries; October 2023 licensing requirements for exports to China and Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Vietnam but excluding Israel; an April 2025 licence requirement for H20 and other circuits above stated thresholds to China, Hong Kong, Macau and D:5 countries or companies ultimately parented there; a May 2025 announcement that the AI Diffusion interim final rule would be rescinded and replaced, with scope, timing and requirements uncertain; controls addressing total processing performance, performance density, interconnect bandwidth and memory bandwidth; licence conditions already imposed that limit foreign firms' ability to create and offer large-scale GPU clusters as a service; licences granted from August 2025 for H20 and from February 2026 for H200 to specified China-based customers whose sales were then restricted by the PRC government, leaving inventory unsold; inventory and purchase-obligation provisions of $1.0 billion for the quarter and $6.3 billion for the half of fiscal 2026, including $4.5 billion for H20 excess inventory; the company's position that export controls have harmed and will further harm its competitive position and have a disproportionate impact on it relative to competitors selling chips outside the controls' scope, with effects in Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia as well as China; assistance provided to authorities on attempted diversion; Data Center revenue of $89.0 billion, up 117% year on year and 18% sequentially; gross margin of 75.0% against 72.4% a year earlier; three direct customers at 16%, 15% and 13% of first-half fiscal 2027 revenue, and two at 23% and 16% in the second quarter of fiscal 2026; and a new business model with select AI cloud partners involving six-year cloud service commitments totalling $36 billion as of 26 July 2026 and a revenue share receivable from those partners if criteria are met.

citations.title: NVIDIA Corporation, Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended 26 July 2026, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission 26 August 2026 (Accession No. 0001045810-26-000075)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov EDGAR (1.5 MB) and read as extracted text; the filing was located through the Commission's own submissions index for CIK 0001045810. (sec.gov serves files to a request declaring an identity and contact address, so automated link checks report sec.gov URLs as blocked.) This is the company's own sworn disclosure, not commentary about it. THE GATEKEEPING, IN THE COMPANY'S WORDS: "We continue to be subject to a series of shifting and expanding export control restrictions, impacting our ability to serve customers outside the United States." The milestones it records: "In August 2022, the USG announced export restrictions and export licensing requirements targeting China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries"; "In October 2023, the USG announced new and updated licensing requirements for exports to China and Country Groups D:1, D:4, and D:5 (including but not limited to, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Vietnam, but excluding Israel)"; "In April 2025, the USG informed us that it requires a license for export to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and D:5 countries, or to companies headquartered or with an ultimate parent therein, of our H20 integrated circuits" and other circuits above stated thresholds; and "In May 2025, the USG announced that it would rescind the AI Diffusion IFR and implement a replacement rule. The scope, timing, and requirements of the forthcoming rule remain uncertain." THE TECHNICAL PARAMETERS OF THE GATE: "The export controls applicable to China are complex and address a variety of parameters, including the total processing performance of a chip, the 'performance density' of a chip, the interconnect bandwidth of a chip, and the memory bandwidth of a chip." THE CONDITION THAT REACHES PAST THE CHIP TO THE SERVICE: "the USG already imposed license conditions that limit the ability of foreign firms to create and offer as a service large-scale GPU clusters, such as imposing license conditions on the use of products to be exported to certain countries". LICENCES GRANTED AND THEN BLOCKED FROM THE OTHER SIDE: "Beginning in August 2025, the USG granted licenses that would have allowed us to ship certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, but such sales were restricted by the PRC government, and we were unable to sell our H20 inventory." And: "Beginning in February 2026, the USG granted licenses that would allow us to ship small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers, but such sales were restricted by the PRC government, and we have been unable to sell all the products for which we have" licences. The cost of that is booked: provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations "totaled $1.0 billion and $6.3 billion for the second quarter and first half of fiscal year 2026, respectively, including $4.5 billion associated with H20 excess inventory". THE COMPANY'S OWN VIEW OF WHO THE CONTROLS HURT: "Our competitive position has been harmed by export controls, and our competitive position and future results will be further harmed, over the long term, if the restrictions remain in place or are expanded"; "Export controls have and are likely in the future to have a disproportionate impact on NVIDIA and may disadvantage us against certain of our competitors that sell chips that are outside the scope of such control"; and the effects reach "not only in China, but also in other markets, such as Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia." On diversion: "We have provided and will continue to provide assistance to authorities regarding attempted diversion". THE SCALE AND THE CONCENTRATION: "Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year ago and up 18% sequentially, driven by the ramp of our Blackwell Ultra infrastructure." Gross margin "increased to 75.0% for the second quarter of fiscal year 2027 compared to 72.4% for the second quarter of fiscal year 2026". On customer concentration: "For the first half of fiscal year 2027, three direct customers represented 16%, 15%, and 13% of total revenue"; for the second quarter of fiscal 2026, "two direct customers represented 23% and 16% of total revenue". THE REVENUE SHARE, AND EXACTLY WHO IT IS WITH: in the second quarter of fiscal 2027 the company "introduced a new business model with certain select AI cloud partners, to enable broader access to our data center infrastructure products to serve AI startups, model builders, enterprises, research organizations" and "sovereign customers". "Under these agreements, AI clouds procure our data center infrastructure products and we commit to cloud service agreements, which the AI clouds can unilaterally stop providing to us and sell to third-party customers at more advantageous rates." Those commitments "are typically six years in duration, totaled $36 billion as of July 26, 2026". And: "If certain criteria are met, we will participate in revenue share generated by the AI clouds from third-party customers, which may contribute to revenue in the future." WHAT THE FULL TEXT DOES NOT CONTAIN, CHECKED BY SEARCH: there is no mention of any payment, remittance or revenue share to the United States government or to any government. The strings "remit", "payment to the U.S", "to the USG" and "equity stake" do not appear. The only "15%" in the filing is a customer-concentration figure. The only revenue share disclosed is with AI cloud partners. Any claim that the company pays a percentage of its China revenue to the United States government is not in this filing, and nothing of the kind is asserted here. Nor does the filing use the word cartel, describe any agreement with competitors, or disclose any antitrust proceeding in the passages read.
